cards.front: Cassandra vs CockroachDB at a glance
cards.back: Cassandra is a leaderless wide-column store with tunable, eventual-by-default consistency, leaning AP. CockroachDB is relational SQL with one Raft group per range and serializable transactions, leaning CP.
The partition key is hashed (Murmur3) to a token on a ring; each node owns several token ranges and the next RF nodes clockwise hold replicas. Nodes learn about each other by gossip, with no master.
The client talks to any node, which forwards to the replicas and waits for as many as the level asks: ONE, QUORUM, ALL, or LOCAL_QUORUM to stay inside one datacenter.

No joins and limited secondary indexes, so you design one table per query, partitioned by what you look up and clustered by how you sort, duplicating data on purpose. Keep partitions under about 100 MB.
IF NOT EXISTS uses Paxos for compare-and-set on one partition, at about four round trips. Use them sparingly.
Every row becomes a key in one sorted key space, cut into ranges of 512 MB by default. Ranges split when they grow or get hot and are rebalanced across nodes, each with its own Raft group.
One replica per range holds a lease and serves reads without a consensus round, since it knows every committed write. It is usually also the Raft leader.

Writes are laid down as intents plus a transaction record; commit flips the record. Keys are versioned (MVCC) with hybrid logical clock timestamps, and conflicting transactions wait or restart, so clients retry serialization errors.
Writes are blind (no read first) and sequential on disk: commit log plus memtable, flushed to SSTables. Reads pay instead, merging a memtable and several SSTables, so compaction strategy matters.

cards.front: When to pick Cassandra vs CockroachDB
cards.back: Cassandra when writes dominate and must never be refused and access patterns are simple and known. CockroachDB when you need multi-row transactions, changing queries with joins, and reads that always reflect committed writes.
A low-cardinality partition key like a country or today's date puts a huge share of traffic on three nodes. Add a bucket to the key, such as (sensor_id, day).
Auto-incrementing primary keys send every insert to the last range, so one node takes every write. Use UUIDs or hash-sharded indexes.

quiz.q: Two clients update the same Cassandra cell concurrently. What happens?
choices: Last write wins by timestamp, silently dropping one
Both values are kept for the app to merge
The write is rejected until a quorum agrees
quiz.why: Cassandra resolves cell conflicts with last write wins, which clock skew can make worse.

quiz.q: A CockroachDB range loses its majority of replicas. What does it do?
choices: Stops serving that range rather than diverge
Keeps serving from the leaseholder alone
quiz.why: CockroachDB leans CP, like any Raft-based store.

quiz.q: Which Cassandra read and write levels make a read see the latest acknowledged write with RF 3?
quiz.why: 2 + 2 > 3, so the read and write sets overlap.

quiz.q: What does a CockroachDB node do if its clock drifts past the maximum offset?
choices: Shuts itself down rather than risk wrong answers
Keeps running and logs a warning
quiz.why: Correct transactions depend on loosely synchronized clocks (500 ms max offset by default).

quiz.q: For a chat app's message history, the page suggests Cassandra with which key design?
choices: Partition by conversation ID plus a time bucket, cluster by message time
quiz.why: Writes dominate and the access pattern is fixed: messages by conversation, newest first.

quiz.q: Many CockroachDB transactions update one global counter. What is the likely symptom?
choices: Contention, with transactions queueing and restarting
quiz.why: Serializable transactions on the same rows conflict and retry.

quiz.q: Which Cassandra compaction strategy suits time series data?
quiz.why: The page lists size-tiered for writes, leveled for reads and time-window for time series.
